Castillo refers to a rust-resistant coffee variety developed by Colombia’s Cenicafé research institute as an improved alternative to Caturra. It is a high-yielding, disease-resistant variety that underpins much of Colombia’s modern coffee production.
SL28 is a Kenyan Arabica variety selected by Scott Laboratories, renowned for its exceptional cup quality with blackcurrant, citrus, and wine-like flavor notes.

SL34 refers to a Kenyan coffee variety selected by Scott Laboratories, closely related to Bourbon and valued for its sweet, complex cup. It is widely grown in Kenya’s highland regions and is a staple of the country’s premium production.

Ruiru 11 refers to a compact, rust-resistant coffee variety developed in Kenya to combine high yield with disease resistance. It produces a cup that is generally considered solid but less celebrated than Kenya’s SL28 and SL34.

Batian refers to a rust-resistant coffee variety released by Kenya’s Coffee Research Institute in 2010. It combines resistance to coffee leaf rust and coffee berry disease with a cup quality that approaches Kenya’s classic SL28 and SL34.
Pacamara is a large-beaned Arabica hybrid from El Salvador, created by crossing Pacas and Maragogipe, known for its complex, nuanced flavor and impressive bean size.
Pacas refers to a natural mutation of the Bourbon variety discovered in El Salvador in the mid-20th century. It is a compact, productive variety that produces a sweet, balanced, crowd-pleasing cup.

Kent refers to a rust-resistant coffee variety selected in India from a Typica planting. It was one of the first widely planted rust-resistant varieties and remains a notable part of India’s coffee history.
Washed (wet) processing removes the coffee cherry fruit before drying, producing clean, bright, and transparent cups that clearly express origin and variety characteristics.
Natural (dry) processing dries whole coffee cherries with the fruit intact, imparting fruity, wine-like, and complex flavors to the beans through extended contact with the fruit.

Pulped natural process refers to removing the skin of the coffee cherry mechanically but leaving some or all of the mucilage on the parchment during drying. The sticky layer’s sugars caramelise on the drying beds, adding sweetness and body to what otherwise remains a clean, parchment-dried coffee. It sits between the washed and natural methods in both flavor impact and water use.
Honey processing removes the cherry skin but leaves varying amounts of mucilage on the bean during drying, producing coffees with sweetness and body between washed and natural.

Wet-hulling refers to stripping the parchment off coffee while it is still moist, then drying the naked green bean in the sun. Removing parchment early — the step that gives the method its Indonesian name, giling basah, “wet grinding” — exposes the bean to the open air at a stage when other methods keep it protected. The result is a cup with low acidity, heavy body, and the earth, spice, and must notes characteristic of Indonesian coffee.

Wet milling refers to the mechanized station where freshly picked coffee cherries are turned into parchment coffee: depulping, fermentation or mechanical demucilaging, washing, and pre-drying all happen in one place. It is the industrial counterpart of the washing station, common in Brazil and Central America where farms deliver cherry directly to a facility. The same words are also used for the milling step that removes parchment from dry coffee, a stage more often called dry milling.

Washing station refers to a facility where smallholder farmers deliver freshly picked coffee cherries for processing into parchment coffee. The station depulps, ferments, washes, and dries the coffee, paying for cherry by weight or by the day’s delivery. In East Africa — Kenya, Ethiopia, Rwanda, Burundi — the washing station is the organizational heart of coffee production, because most growers own too little land to process coffee themselves.
Mucilage is the sticky, sugar-rich layer surrounding the coffee bean inside the cherry, which plays a key role in fermentation and flavor development during processing.

Double fermentation refers to a coffee processing variation in which the mucilage is removed in two separate ferment stages rather than one. The classic Kenyan method ferments the depulped coffee until the mucilage loosens, washes it, then soaks the clean parchment in fresh water for a second, longer period. The second soak polishes the bean and deepens the clarity, sparkle, and complexity for which Kenyan washed coffee is known.

Yungas is a coffee-producing region of steep cloud-forest valleys on the eastern slope of the Andes in Bolivia, running from the Altiplano down toward the Amazon basin. It is the country’s historic and principal coffee region, with plantings between roughly 1,000 and 2,000 meters along the famous “Camino de la Muerte” road from La Paz. Altitude, mild temperatures, and cloud cover give Yungas coffee its balanced acidity, caramel sweetness, and smooth body.

Tarrazú is a coffee-producing region in the highlands south of San José, Costa Rica, centered on the town of San Marcos. It is one of the world’s most recognizable coffee appellations, with farms between roughly 1,200 and 1,900 meters on slopes that face the Pacific. High altitude, distinct wet and dry seasons, and rich volcanic soil produce a bright, aromatic cup with crisp citric acidity and a clean finish.

Central Valley is a coffee-producing region in the heart of Costa Rica, the basin around the capital San José that includes Heredia and Alajuela. It was the country’s first commercial coffee region and remains one of its most planted, with farms between roughly 900 and 1,500 meters on slopes with distinct wet and dry seasons. Volcanic soil and reliable dry-season harvest windows give a balanced cup with chocolate notes, gentle fruit, and bright acidity.

West Valley is a coffee-producing region in Costa Rica, the Pacific-facing hills west of San José around Naranjo, Palmares, Sarchí, and Grecia. It is known for late harvests — the dry season arrives later than elsewhere in the country — and for a long record of Cup of Excellence wins. Farms between roughly 900 and 1,600 meters produce a sweet, balanced cup with citric acidity and caramel and stone-fruit notes.

Naranjo is a coffee-producing canton in Costa Rica’s West Valley, one of the country’s most decorated coffee sub-regions. Farms on its Pacific-facing slopes between roughly 1,100 and 1,700 meters have taken repeated Cup of Excellence honors, on lots dominated by Villa Sarchí and Caturra alongside Catuai. The cup profile is balanced and sweet with citric acidity and stone-fruit and caramel notes.

Apaneca-Ilamatepec is a coffee-producing mountain range in western El Salvador, part of the volcanic chain that runs through Central America and one of the coffee world’s storied names. Coffee grows on the slopes of the Santa Ana volcano between roughly 1,000 and 1,700 meters, where volcanic soil and Bourbon-led plantings produce a sweet, balanced cup with gentle acidity and notes of caramel, cocoa, and citrus.

Bolaven Plateau is a coffee-producing region of southern Laos, a fertile volcanic plateau rising between roughly 800 and 1,300 meters above the Mekong lowlands. Planted largely to robusta with a growing arabica share, it produces nearly all of Laos’s commercial coffee. Cooler plateau air and basalt soil give its best arabicas a mild, balanced cup, while the robusta underpins regional blends and instant coffee.

Mount Kilimanjaro is a coffee-producing region on the slopes of Africa’s highest mountain in northeastern Tanzania, between roughly 900 and 1,800 meters on the southern and eastern faces. Smallholder gardens shaded by banana groves dominate, intercropped in the Chagga tradition of the mountain’s foothills. Volcanic soils, abundant springs, and altitude combine for a clean, balanced cup with gentle acidity and fruity sweetness.

Coffee Triangle is a coffee-producing region in Colombia — the axis of Caldas, Risaralda, and Quindío, with Tolima and Antioquia often included — where the Andes split into three cordilleras. It is the heart of Colombian coffee culture: rolling hills at 1,300 to 1,900 meters, small family farms on steep slopes, and the UNESCO-listed Coffee Cultural Landscape. Colombia’s washed arabicas, fermented clean and sun-dried, made the region’s name on clarity, sweetness, and consistency.

Doi Tung is a coffee-producing mountain in Chiang Rai province, northern Thailand, near the borders with Myanmar and Laos. It is the site of the royal development project that replaced opium poppy with arabica coffee in the late 1980s, part of the Doi Tung Development Programme. Plantings at roughly 1,000 to 1,600 meters under shade are mostly Catimor, with expanding Bourbon and Typica shares as quality ambitions rise.

Doi Chang is a coffee-producing mountain village in Chiang Rai province, northern Thailand, home to an Akha community whose village-run coffee company exports its own single-origin arabica. Coffee grows at roughly 1,200 to 1,600 meters under shade, mostly Catimor with Bourbon and Typica plantings, and the village’s success made it one of Thailand’s best-known specialty names.

Cafecito refers to a small cup of strong, sweet coffee — the everyday coffee ritual of Cuba and the Cuban diaspora. It is brewed as a concentrated moka-pot or espresso-style shot and sweetened directly, often with demerara sugar, then served in a tacita, a tiny cup, at home, at ventanitas, and at any hour. Sharing cafecito is the gesture of hospitality itself: to be offered one is to be included.

Espuma refers to the creamy, tan froth that crowns sweetened coffee made in the Cuban style. Sugar is whipped with the first draw of strong coffee into a pale paste, then folded back through the pot so that aerated foam floats on the finished cup, adding texture and sweetness while carrying aroma. A visible crown of espuma is the mark of a well-made colada or cafecito.

Phin refers to a small metal coffee filter used throughout Vietnam and the tool behind cà phê sữa đá. A perforated plate sits over the cup, ground coffee goes inside, a weighted press screws down on the grounds, and hot water drips through the chamber straight into the cup below, one bead at a time. The slow drip over dark-roast robusta, poured onto ice and condensed milk, defines Vietnamese coffee.

Monsooned Malabar refers to coffee from the Malabar Coast of India that is deliberately exposed to monsoon winds after processing, a curing method that transforms the bean. Green coffee is stored in open-sided warehouses where moist monsoon air swells the beans over weeks, mellowing acidity to almost nothing, turning the beans pale gold, and producing a cup with heavy body and notes of must, spice, and wood.

Blue Mountain Coffee is a coffee-producing region and appellation in the Blue Mountains of Jamaica, above roughly 1,000 meters within a legally defined zone on the island’s eastern end. It is one of the world’s most protected names in coffee: certified under Jamaica’s coffee appellation system, shipped in the trademark wooden barrel, and made up almost entirely of a Typica selection known as the Blue Mountain cultivar.
